user_turns:
My boyfriend has been putting off getting a dog for two years. "After we renew the lease." "After Portugal." Then in March it was "maybe next year, let me get my exams done first." He found out he'd passed them on September 18th. Two years of excuses.

I've volunteered at a dog rescue on Saturday mornings since May. Pepper is three, she's the sweetest thing, and her foster family could only keep her until October 4th. If nobody took her by then, she was going to the kennel. I showed Callum her picture that Wednesday and he said, "She's cute." On Saturday I brought her home. He was at his brother's for the weekend, so I texted him a photo.

He got home Sunday, said "I said next year," and told me she goes back before the return window closes on the 17th. He won't walk her or feed her. He says she's my dog and he's not doing any of it. Fine, I'm doing all of it.

I'm hurt, and honestly I feel like an idiot for waiting this long. He strung me along, and I think he just likes having a veto on everything in this house.

Am I wrong to want to keep her?

results.result:
Wanting to keep her isn't wrong. You've wanted a dog for two years, you've put in months at the rescue, and Pepper needed somewhere to go. That's a real and reasonable want, and your hurt makes sense. Two years of "after X" is a long time to wait, especially when the last condition he named, his exams, was met weeks before you brought her home.

But wanting her and how she arrived are two different questions, and I think you know the second one is shakier. You brought a dog into a shared home while he was away, after he'd said "she's cute" (which isn't a yes) and "next year." Even if his delays were frustrating, that move did exactly what you're accusing him of: one person deciding for the household. That's probably why he's dug in so hard. Right now he may be reacting less to Pepper and more to feeling overruled.

That doesn't make him right. If he's never going to want a dog, he owes you that honestly instead of a rolling "later." And refusing to touch her while she's in the house feels more like making a point than handling a disagreement.

You have five days before the 17th, so here's what I'd do:

- **Own your part first.** Something like "I shouldn't have brought her home without a real yes from you. I was frustrated and I jumped." It costs you little, and it may be the only thing that gets him out of defensive mode.
- **Then ask the real question.** "Is this about timing, or do you not want a dog at all?" If it's timing, what would a concrete yes look like? A date? A condition? If it's never, that's a much bigger conversation than Pepper.
- **Get specific about his objections.** Money, mess, travel, the lease, being tied down? Some of these can be solved, and you can't solve the ones you don't know about.
- **Think about Pepper either way.** If she goes back, could the rescue place her with another foster instead of the kennel? Ask them now so you're not deciding under pressure on the 16th.

The question underneath this one is the one you raised yourself: does he hold a veto over everything in your home? If that's a pattern beyond the dog, it's worth naming directly. Just raise it on its own, not as part of the Pepper fight, where it'll look like ammunition.

What do you think his real hesitation is?

Partly, and I don't want to just tell you what you want to hear.

You're right that your want is reasonable, that two years of moving goalposts is unfair, and that he owes you a straight answer about whether he wants a dog at all.

You're not right that bringing her home while he was away was okay. That was a unilateral decision about a shared home, the same kind of move you're upset with him for. If he'd done something equivalent, like signing up for something major you'd both live with while you were away, you'd feel steamrolled too.

Both things are true at once, and that's the useful part. If you go into this conversation trying to prove you're right, he'll defend himself and Pepper likely goes back on the 17th with nothing resolved. If you admit the misstep and then press hard on the real issue, whether "later" ever means yes, you're in a much stronger position, both for Pepper and for the bigger pattern you're worried about.
